An illustrated step-by-step manual with screenshots — saved into your Downloads and opened, so it stays on the phone
A quick tour of every screen. The five main ones can be swiped through as well as tapped in the bottom bar. Everything works offline; data leaves the phone only if you switch on cloud sync.

Kosht works without an account, and your records stay on the phone. An account is for one thing: seeing the same figures on your other phone.
At first launch you can create one, sign in, or carry on without it. Signing up asks for your email, sends a six-digit code to it, and then lets you pick a password. Forgot it later? The same code arrives by email and you set a new one.
After that everything happens by itself: records, categories, accounts, debts, goals, challenges and awards appear on your other phone as soon as you sign in there. No connection is needed to keep working — whatever you add offline goes up the moment the internet is back. Deleting something deletes it everywhere, so nothing you removed comes back.
Settings → Account shows the address, when it last synced, a button to sync right now, a switch for doing it automatically, and Sign out — which leaves every record on the phone. Receipt photos are never uploaded.
Your settings travel too: currency, theme, the interface and notification switches, the daily budget, the report you built, your name and nickname. A second phone ends up looking and behaving like the first. The interface language stays with the device, on purpose.
Receipt photos are the exception, and they are off by default — the policy says the images stay on the phone, and they do until you say otherwise. Switch on "Sync receipt photos" in the Account block and they are uploaded to a private folder only your account can read, and downloaded onto your other device. That switch is a consent of its own and is recorded as one; switching it off deletes the uploaded copies and leaves the originals here.
The sync icon sits in the row with your address: it starts a sync and turns into a spinner while one is running. Tap the row itself for the full address, the exact time of the last sync and whether automatic sync is on.

The big card shows your total balance (all income minus all expenses) with this month\'s income and expenses below it. If your currency is not BYN, the ≈ line shows the equivalent at the live rate. In the top row: the 🔥 chip is your under-budget streak, the trophy opens Achievements, and the avatar opens your profile — the same dialog Settings opens, so a name or a picture can be changed right where you are looking at it. The app deals itself one of the built-in avatars on the very first launch, so there is a face there from the start; pick another and yours is the one that stays. "Recent" lists the latest records — tap one to edit, "All" jumps to History. The big + button adds a transaction.

Switch Expense/Income at the top, or swipe sideways across the amount — the same gesture that moves the app\'s own tabs. For a new record the calculator opens by itself in a bottom sheet; type the sum (comma adds cents) and hit Apply — tap the amount any time to open it again. Pick a category in the carousel — the "New" circle creates your own with a name, icon and color. Press and hold one and it comes off the row: drag it to where it belongs and the new order is kept everywhere, or let go without moving and the category opens for correcting — name, icon, color, or the trash, which moves its records to "Other" rather than losing them. Instead of an icon from the set you can pick a photo from the gallery, the logo of a payment app or a shop: it fills the circle wherever the category appears, and the palette steps aside while it is there. A name too long for its tile is cut with an ellipsis — tap the category and it is spelled out in full above the row. Income filed under "Debt" asks one more thing, who the money is owed to, and opens that debt on the Wallet tab with the note you wrote. The date chip opens a calendar (defaults to today). Write an optional note. Under the carousel is a row of chips, each with a word on it: the date, the account the money leaves (it appears once you keep more than one), the basket that lists what was bought — expenses only, see "Products in a record" — "Scan receipt", the electronic receipt when the slip came with one, and the photo, which turns into a thumbnail once something is attached; tap it to view or remove. A record whose figures came off a receipt says so under the amount and carries a small scanner mark in every list. Save finishes. When editing an existing record a trash icon appears in the top bar, and the account can be changed there like everything else.

Most categories only sort money. Four of them also move something in the Wallet, and they are the only ones that do.
"Debt" among income: the editor asks one more thing — who the money is owed to — and saving opens that debt on the Wallet tab, in the currency of the app, with your note on it.
"Debt repaid" among expenses: the Wallet writes this record itself when you repay or close a debt there with "record in history" ticked. The record and the debt stay tied to each other.
"To savings" among expenses and "From savings" among income: the same pair for the piggy bank. The Wallet writes them when you put money aside or take it back with "take from the account" ticked, so the money leaves the balance once and the savings only once.
The tie matters when a record goes. Delete the one that repaid a debt and the debt comes back with that amount and the day it was first written down — reopened if the repayment had closed it. Delete the one that opened a debt and the debt goes with it. Undo in the snackbar puts both sides back as they were.
The four are recognised by what they are, not by what they are called, so rename them, recolour them or give them a picture — the action stays. Delete one and its records move to "Other": from then on they are ordinary records and move nothing.

In the editor tap "Scan receipt", then shoot the slip or pick it from the gallery. Reading takes a few seconds — the line above says so while it works.
If the receipt has a QR code, Kosht reads the shop\'s electronic receipt through it — the figures come out exact, and even a slip with nothing but a QR on it works. That receipt is saved, and the receipt icon in the editor opens it again later, with or without a connection. When the page offers the receipt as a file to download, Kosht takes the file itself rather than the page around it, and that is what the icon opens. A code that turns out to be a loyalty card or an advert is skipped. A code is rarely in the middle of the picture, so the photo is searched in overlapping squares, each tried the right way up, upside down and inverted, and Data Matrix and bar codes are tried as well as QR.
With no QR the photo itself is read, right on the phone. Either way a dialog shows what was found: correct the amount or the shop if needed, the date fills itself in. Apply puts everything into the form, and you can still change any of it afterwards.
The shop goes into the note. A familiar chain is recognised by name; an unfamiliar one is read off the way the slip is printed — the largest type at the top, a trade name in quotes, a legal form, the line beside the tax number. Addresses, cashiers, document headers, card details and scanning noise are thrown out, and a line that no shop would print — longer than the note field takes — is left out entirely rather than cut in half: the note then simply stays empty.
The reading is helped along before it starts, in the middle, and after. A slip photographed by hand is never lit evenly — half in shadow, half blown out — so every dot is compared with the average of the paper around it rather than with one brightness for the whole picture, and a small photo is enlarged. The page is then read several ways, each scored on how sure the recognition was and how many prices came out, and the best reading wins; a clearly good one stops the rest early. Afterwards the letters recognition mistakes for digits are put right: a price printed as "1,4О" or "l2,50" is a price, and only inside something already shaped like an amount, so names keep their letters and no figure is invented. All of it happens on the phone, with nothing sent anywhere.
The slip\'s own lines are read as well. When the receipt lists what was bought, the review dialog says how many products it found, and they land in the record\'s product list — including the quantity where the line printed one. Discounts, VAT, card details and the total itself are not products and are left out. The list is yours to correct afterwards in the basket chip.
What decides which line is which is a small AI model that ships inside the app — 77 KB of weights trained on Belarusian slips and on the mistakes recognition makes on them. It runs on the phone, needs no account, no key and no connection, and nothing leaves the device. It is asked where rules alone are not enough: which line settles a slip that never prints the word "total", which line in the header is the shop, and whether a line that looks like a purchase really names one. Where the slip does say "к оплате" the plain rule still wins — the model is there for the awkward ones.

Arrows switch months. The search field filters by note and custom category names. Chips: All / Expense / Income, "Category" opens a category picker (tap ✕ on the chip to clear), "Period" opens a calendar where you select a single day or a range — the period replaces month navigation until you clear it with ✕. Records are grouped by day with a net total per day. Swipe a row left to delete — an Undo snackbar appears. Tap a row to edit it.
Swiping a row deletes it and offers it back: "Transaction deleted — Undo" appears along the bottom, always above the add button, and the same offer follows a delete from the editor. The receipt photo is only thrown away once that offer has passed, so undoing really does put everything back.

Three views via the round buttons: 1) Charts — a donut of categories with the total in the middle and daily bars below; 2) Calendar — a heatmap where a darker day means more spent; tap a day to see its records; 3) Report — the verdict for a whole period, with arrows walking back through past ones. It shows spending vs the previous period of the same length, income, result, daily average, no-spend days, top category and personalized tips. Which period it covers (week, month, quarter, year) and which rows are shown are set in Settings → Report. The Expense/Income toggle applies to charts and calendar, arrows switch months. Under the category list the Products block appears as soon as any record of the month lists what was bought — income too, since a salary can be split into the pay and the bonus: every product with what it cost you in total, how much of the shopping that is and how many records mention it. One product is one row however it was typed: case and stray spaces are ignored, and ё reads as е. Transfers between your own accounts are left out of every figure here — moving money is neither spending nor earning.

The NBRB rates card shows official rates with the update time — the arrow button refreshes them manually; without a connection the rates from the last successful check stay on screen and a toast explains why nothing changed. Any amount in a foreign currency shows its ≈ BYN equivalent. Changing the app currency in Settings converts all stored amounts at the current rate; each expense also freezes its BYN value at payment time, so history never drifts. Planned payments: + adds one — Expense or Income (a salary is as regular as a subscription), title, amount, currency, the date picked in a calendar, a frequency (weekly / monthly / every 3 months / yearly), a category and, with several accounts, the account it moves on. The dialog reads the way the money goes: a bill has a title, an amount to charge and a charge date, a salary a source, a sum and the date it lands. Nothing is charged silently: due payments appear in "Awaiting confirmation", and Confirm records the movement — the dialog says which way it goes, starts from the account the plan names and lets you adjust both the amount and, for a foreign currency, the rate. Tap a payment to change any of it, the switch pauses it, the trash deletes it.

Debts: + adds one — who, direction (I owe / owed to me), amount in any currency, note. The two tiles total both directions in BYN. Tap a debt to repay a part, close it or delete it — and the pencil in that dialog opens the debt itself for correcting: the person, the direction, the sum, the currency, the note. Money that changes hands lands in the history as well: an expense for what you owed, income for what was owed to you, marked as the debt closed or a part of it. The tick above the buttons is what decides — clear it for a debt settled outside the app — and with several accounts you say which one it moved on.
Goals: + creates a goal with a target amount; deposits linked to the goal fill its progress bar, and reaching the target celebrates 🎉. Tap a goal to change any of it — the name, the target, the currency it is counted in — with the trash in the corner of that dialog. Changing the currency carries what is already set aside toward it across at the official rate, so the progress bar keeps meaning what it says.
Savings: "Set aside" and "Withdraw" record movements (optionally toward a goal), the journal below lists them with BYN equivalents; the trash removes an entry. The sum can be in any currency: pick it in the chips and Kosht converts it into the currency the savings are counted in — the app\'s, or the goal\'s — at the National Bank rate. That converted figure sits in its own field, and it is editable: the bank\'s arithmetic and the official rate rarely agree to the last kopeck, and what actually left the account is what should be written down. Savings are counted apart from the accounts, so by default nothing else moves; tick «Take it off an account» and the sum really leaves the one you pick — as an expense when you set it aside, as income back onto it when you withdraw — so the balance follows the jar.

Open with the trophy on Home. The streak card counts consecutive days you stayed within the daily budget (set it in Settings, auto = last month\'s average). Challenges: + creates one — Limit (spend under X, optionally in one category), No spend, or Save up (set aside X) — for a week, until month end or 30 days. Progress updates live; tap a challenge to edit its title, amount, category and end date, the trash removes it. Below are 30 awards, six to a page, easiest first: from the first record to a year inside the budget, a thousand records, five thousand saved, a perfect month without a single day over budget, three months in a row in the black, and twenty challenges completed. Tap any award to see how to earn it, your progress toward it (like "6 / 10"), and the date you earned it. An award unlocks the moment it is deserved, whichever screen you are on: a congratulation appears over the app and a quiet note lands in the shade — you never have to open this screen for it to count. Once earned an award stays yours forever, even if the streak resets.

By default there is a single account and the app looks perfectly simple. Add more (Settings → Accounts: name, icon, color — e.g. Cash, a second card) and Kosht lights up: the editor gets an account chip next to the date so you choose where the money comes from or goes to, confirming a recurring payment asks which account to deduct from, Home shows a balance pill per account under the main card, and Statistics gains an account filter. Tapping an account opens its card: the pencil (or a tap on the name) reveals renaming plus icon and color — or a picture of your own from the gallery, the same as a category — the balance field sets the real amount, and the trash icon deletes it — its records move to the primary account. The ⇄ button next to + moves money between two of them; see "Transfers between accounts".

Withdrawing cash from a card, or topping one card up from another, is not spending — the money is still yours. So Kosht records it as a transfer: on Wallet, in the Accounts block, the ⇄ button opens the dialog (it appears once you keep more than one account).
Pick where from and where to, the amount, the date and an optional note. The amount leaves the source account and lands on the destination one; your total balance does not move, and no chart, category, streak, challenge or report counts it as an expense or an income. In History and on Home a transfer shows with its own ⇄ icon and reads "Card → Cash".
Switch on Settings → Interface → "Transfer fee" and the dialog gains a fee field, for the cases where moving money costs something. The fee comes off the source account on top of the amount — it is the one part of a transfer that really does leave your pocket, so the total balance drops by exactly that much. The dialog spells out what will be taken off the account, and the row in the lists says "fee 1,50" next to the date.
Tap a transfer in any list to correct it or delete it — the same dialog opens, with Delete in place of Cancel, and the usual Undo offer follows. Deleting an account also deletes the transfers that ran between it and the account inheriting its records: those would have ended up going from itself to itself.

A record can say what the money went on, not just how much of it went. The basket chip in the editor opens the list: type a product, optionally what it cost and how many, and Add puts it in. Tap a line to correct it, ✕ removes it. Names you have used before are offered as chips while you type — tapping one keeps the spelling identical. Typing it differently is no great loss either: the statistics fold case and stray spaces together, so "молоко", "Молоко " and "МОЛОКО" stay one product with one total.
Nothing here is required. A record with no list is complete, the chip stays quiet until you use it, and the amount of the record is never overwritten by what the lines add up to — the list is a description of the purchase, not a second source of truth.
Scanning a receipt fills the list in by itself where the slip lists its lines (see "Receipt scanning"), quantities included.
What it is for: Statistics → Charts → Products shows every product of the month with what it cost you in total, how many times it turned up and how much of the month\'s shopping it is. That is where "we spend how much on coffee?" gets an answer.

The calculator lives in a full-width bottom sheet: it opens by itself for a new record and whenever you tap the amount. The right column of the keypad holds ÷ × − +. Type expressions like 12,50+3,90+8. While an operation is unfinished the big button turns into = — tap it to evaluate. Apply writes the result into the amount field and closes the sheet; Cancel or a swipe down leaves the amount untouched. Multiplication and division take precedence, as they should.

Kosht can ask for a code before it opens: Settings → Security → "App lock". Make up 4 to 8 digits, repeat them, and that is the lock on.
The code is typed on the app\'s own keypad and shown as dots — never as digits, so a glance over your shoulder gets nothing. It is not kept anywhere as a code either: only a deliberately slow one-way digest of it, salted with random bytes of its own, which is why nobody can look it up or send it back to you (see "Forgot the code?" on the lock screen).
If the phone has a finger or a face on file, "Unlock with biometrics" appears. Switching it on asks for the finger once, to prove it works before you rely on it. After that the sensor key sits in the keypad itself — bottom left, under your thumb — and the phone\'s own prompt comes up by itself the moment the lock appears; dismiss it and the code still works.
Four wrong codes cost nothing. From the fifth the keypad goes cold, and each try after that waits longer — half a minute, a minute, five, fifteen — counted on disk, so force-closing the app does not hand the attempts back. A finger is never made to wait: a fingerprint is not a guess.
"Ask for the code" decides how long being away counts for — type the number of minutes yourself, or tap "As soon as you leave" for none at all. Whatever it says, a screen Kosht opened itself — the camera, the gallery, the install-permission page — is not treated as leaving; photographing a receipt should not cost you a code.
With the lock on, the task switcher stops keeping a picture of the app, so the balance is not readable there either. And the code stays on this phone: it is kept apart from the settings that travel, so a second device never receives it and sets its own.

Profile — tap to set a photo from the gallery or one of the built-in avatars, press and hold the avatar to remove the photo, and set your name and nickname (used in greetings and reports). Interface toggles hide anything you do not need, control whether the calculator opens by itself when adding a record, whether a transfer between accounts offers a fee field. The Report block sets the period the statistics report covers and ticks off exactly which metric rows it shows. Security puts a code between the phone and your figures, with the phone\'s own fingerprint to save the typing — see “App lock”. Notifications: an evening reminder (only if nothing was logged), payments awaiting confirmation, a Monday summary, awards you earn, and — once signed in — whether Kosht may email you about new features. Each of them arrives with the phone\'s notification sound and a short vibration; Android\'s own per-channel settings can quiet any of them down again. The Account block follows: tap the address row to see the full address, the exact time of the last sync and whether automatic sync is on; sign out asks first. Deleting the account and its data no longer sits next to it — one is a door and the other a demolition — it waits at the very bottom of the screen under "Point of no return", with a confirmation of its own. About holds the guide, the Terms, the Personal data policy and the full manual — each tap saves the PDF into your phone\'s Downloads and opens it, so it stays yours to read, print or forward. When either document gets a new version, Kosht says so on the next launch and offers both right there rather than leaving you to notice it here. Tap Version to check for a newer build: Kosht either says you are up to date or downloads and installs the update right there — no browser, nothing left in Downloads, and your data stays in place. Android asks once for permission to let Kosht install its own updates. Offline it just says the check is not possible right now. Theme: system/light/dark plus Material You dynamic colors. Language: system, Russian or English. Currency — switching converts everything at the live NBRB rate: records, the daily budget, balance corrections, challenge limits, savings, goals, debts and recurring charges. Daily budget powers the streak.
The six screens a new user is shown
The + button opens the editor: the calculator asks for the sum, you pick a category, Save writes it down. Expense or income — the switch at the top, or a swipe sideways across the amount.
Photograph the receipt instead of typing
"Scan receipt" reads the slip on the phone itself: a small AI model finds the total, the shop and the items. A QR code on the slip is followed to the electronic receipt.
Home with the balance, History, Statistics, Wallet, Settings. Swipe sideways or press the bottom row.
Accounts and transfers between them, regular payments (never charged behind your back — you confirm each one), debts, goals and savings.
Some categories do more than count
Income filed under "Debt" opens a debt in the Wallet; "Debt repaid" and "To savings" pay one off and top the other up. Delete such a record and whatever it moved comes back.
A streak, and awards for it
Days spent inside your daily budget build a streak, and achievements arrive on their own. The full manual lives in Settings → Guide.
